## Problem 1

Suppose I recruit a sample of $n$ teachers to study the effect of hydration and sleep
on voice quality. Define the following variables:

- $H_i$ is the harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) of the $i$th participant's voice.
This is a measure of voice quality and is measured in decibels.
- $S_i = 1$ if participant $i$ slept well the night before they were assessed and
$S_i = 0$ if they slept poorly.
- $W_i$ is the number of liters of water the $i$th participant drank in
the previous 24 hours.

Suppose I fit the following model:
$$
H_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \beta_2 W_i + \beta_3 S_i W_i + \epsilon_i \text{.}
$$
Please answer the following questions,
assuming all necessary assumptions are met.

### Part (a)

(4 points)
What does $\beta_0$ mean in real-world terms?

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
HNR (1 point) for a teacher who slept poorly the night before (1 point)
and drank no water (1 point) in the past 24 hours.

:::

### Part (b)

(7 points)
Compute $E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w)$
and interpret its meaning in real-world terms.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

$$
\begin{align*}
    &E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 w + \beta_3 (1) w - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 w + \beta_3 (0) w\right) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2 w + \beta_3  w - \left(\beta_0  + \beta_2 w \right) \\
    &= \beta_1 + \beta_3 w \text{ (1 point)}
\end{align*}
$$

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
between those who slept well (1 point)
and those who slept poorly (1 point),
among people who drank $w$ liters of water (1 point) over the past 24 hours.

:::

### Part (c)

(7 points)
Compute $E(H_1 |S_i = 0,W_i = w + 1) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w)$
and interpret its meaning in real-world terms.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

$$
\begin{align*}
    &E(H_1 |S_i = 0,W_i = w + 1) - E(H_i|S_i = 0,W_i = w) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (w+1) + \beta_3 (0) (w+1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (0) + \beta_2 (w) + \beta_3 (0) w \right) \\
    &= \beta_0  + \beta_2 w + \beta_2   - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_2 w  \right) \\
    &= \beta_2 \text{ (1 point)}
\end{align*}
$$

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
change (or increase; 1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
associated with a one-liter increase (1 point)
in water consumption (1 point),
among people who slept poorly (1 point).

Alternatively,
the expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
between two populations of teachers
that differ by one liter (1 point)
in their water consumption (1 point)
but who all slept poorly (1 point).

:::

### Part (d)

Compute $E(H_1 |S_i = 1,W_i = w + 1) - E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w)$
and interpret its meaning in real-world terms.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

$$
\begin{align*}
    &E(H_1 |S_i = 1,W_i = w + 1) - E(H_i|S_i = 1,W_i = w) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (w+1) + \beta_3 (1) (w+1) - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1 (1) + \beta_2 (w) + \beta_3 (1) w \right) \\
    &= \beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2 w + \beta_2 + \beta_3 w + \beta_3 - \left(\beta_0 + \beta_1  + \beta_2 w + \beta_3  w \right) \\
    &= \beta_2 + \beta_3 \text{ (1 point)}
\end{align*}
$$

The expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
change (or increase; 1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
associated with a one-liter increase (1 point)
in water consumption (1 point),
among people who slept well (1 point).

Alternatively,
the expected (or average, or mean, or estimated; 1 point)
difference (1 point)
in HNR (1 point)
between two populations of teachers
that differ by one liter (1 point)
in their water consumption (1 point)
but who all slept well (1 point).

:::

## Problem 2

Please identify each of the following statements as true or false.
Each problem is worth one point.
You do not need to justify your answers.

### Part (a)

We usually consider parameters to be unknown.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (b)

A statistic is a function of the population.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (c)

We use the sample to draw conclusions about the population.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (d)

If you know the expected value of $X$, you should be able to compute the
probability that $X$ is in any given range.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::

### Part (e)

A statistic can have a distribution.

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

True.

:::

### Part (f)

"Statistic" is another word for "parameter."

::: {.callout-tip title="Solution" collapse="true"}

False.

:::
